newsitem.title: UK: Telecom deregulation spawns heavyweight alliances.
newsitem.headline: Telecom deregulation spawns heavyweight alliances.

text.p: The world telecommunications industry, one of the world's fastest moving markets, is undergoing a revolution as global alliances gather muscle to fight for growth amid deregulation and increased competition.

The biggest packs of international telecoms alliances are very large indeed -- British Telecommunications has teamed up with America's MCI to form Concert; the French and German national telecoms companies have linked with Sprint of the United States to form Global One.
And AT&T has set up World Partners with 16 companies.

With alliances such as Sunday's estimated $20 billion BT/MCI merger becoming increasingly powerful, some analysts say only a small number of "super-carriers" will survive the shake-out to become truly global players.

Reversing U.S. policy that in 1984 saw the break-up of national telecoms giant AT&T, President Bill Clinton signed the Telecommunications Act in February, removing barriers between cable, local and long-distance phone services, the United States has become the world's biggest telecoms market.

Under the new law, seven regional "Baby Bell" operators spun off from AT&T can compete with long-distance carriers in the $200 billion U.S. market. It also grants access to the local- call market to AT&T, MCI and Sprint, the three dominant long-distance carriers.
Britain has been following in America's liberalisation footsteps.
In June, the British government said it was ending the duopoly between BT and Cable and Wireless's Mercury unit as international telecommunications carriers from Britain.
Britain said it would invite applications to provide international services -- an opportunity immediately leapt upon by AT&T which said it looked forward to getting a licence.
The rest of Europe is also not far behind -- although some states have been accused of dragging their feet.
But all members of the European Union, plus Switzerland and Norway, are officially preparing to open their doors to competition by the beginning of 1998.
In the Far East, the Japanese government is considering whether to break up Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, the state-owned monopoly and the world's largest telephone group.
China, the Philippines and Malaysia are also inviting competition for their existing services.
